common_name: Dapple Dandy Pluot (Dinosaur Egg Red-Fleshed Plum-Apricot Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Dapple Dandy, nicknamed the Dinosaur Egg, is a Zaiger Genetics pluot (a plum-apricot interspecific hybrid predominantly plum) needing a second plum or pluot pollinator nearby for good fruit set.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and provide a compatible plum or pluot pollinator such as Santa Rosa or Flavor Supreme, since Dapple Dandy is not reliably self-fruitful. Bred by Floyd Zaiger, this pluot, an interspecific plum-apricot hybrid weighted mostly toward its plum parentage, is instantly recognizable by its greenish-yellow skin dappled with maroon-red splotches, which gave rise to its Dinosaur Egg nickname, and by the vivid magenta-red flesh inside that is exceptionally sweet with a rich, complex flavor many tasters rate among the best of the pluot varieties. Fruit ripens over a fairly long midsummer window, giving a spread-out harvest rather than one concentrated picking, and the tree is otherwise managed much like a standard plum, with dormant pruning to an open center and thinning of heavy fruit sets to improve size. Its moderate chill requirement fits mild-winter Southern gardens better than many traditional European plums.

common_name: Flavor Grenade Pluot (Firm Late-Season Green Plum-Apricot Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Flavor Grenade is a Zaiger Genetics pluot bred for exceptionally firm flesh and a long shelf life, and needs a second plum or pluot pollinator nearby for good fruit set.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and plant a second plum or pluot variety nearby for pollination, since Flavor Grenade sets fruit poorly on its own. Another of the Zaiger Genetics pluot introductions, Flavor Grenade keeps its green skin even at full ripeness, which can make judging harvest timing tricky for gardeners used to color-based cues, but the crisp, exceptionally firm, deep red-streaked flesh holds its sugary, tangy-sweet flavor for days after picking better than most stone fruit, making it a favorite for gardeners who want fruit that doesn't turn to mush a day after ripening. It ripens later in the season than most pluots, extending stone fruit harvest into late summer, and the moderately vigorous tree is managed and pruned much like a standard plum. Thin heavy fruit sets in late spring to improve final fruit size.

common_name: Spice Zee Nectaplum (Genetic Dwarf Nectarine-Plum Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Spice Zee is a Zaiger Genetics genetic dwarf nectaplum (nectarine-plum hybrid) that stays small enough for a large container, with striking reddish-purple spring foliage and self-fertile fruit.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; bred by Floyd Zaiger, Spice Zee is a genetic dwarf nectaplum, a nectarine-plum interspecific hybrid, that naturally stays compact enough for a large patio container or small-yard planting while still bearing full-sized, sweet, richly flavored fruit with a flavor many describe as somewhere between a nectarine and a plum. The reddish-purple young foliage in spring, aging to bronze-green, makes it an attractive small ornamental tree even outside of fruiting season, and its self-fertile flowers mean a single tree can set a full crop without a second pollinator. Fruit ripens in early summer, and the naturally dense, rounded canopy benefits from light annual thinning to keep light reaching the interior and to manage fruit size.

common_name: Let's Dance Rhythmic Blue Hydrangea (Compact Reblooming Mophead Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Let's Dance Rhythmic Blue is a Proven Winners reblooming bigleaf hydrangea that flowers on both old and new wood, giving a longer bloom season than older mophead varieties that bloom only on the prior year's growth.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, with protection from hot afternoon sun in the Gulf South. Let's Dance Rhythmic Blue is part of the Proven Winners Let's Dance series of reblooming bigleaf hydrangeas, bred to flower reliably on new growth as well as on old wood, so a late freeze that damages the previous year's stems doesn't wipe out the whole season's bloom the way it can on older mophead cultivars. Its compact, rounded habit fits smaller foundation plantings and containers better than full-sized mopheads, and the large, rounded flower clusters shift from blue to pink depending on soil pH, staying truest blue in acidic soil amended with aluminum sulfate if needed. Deadhead spent blooms and prune lightly to shape in late winter, avoiding heavy pruning that would remove the current season's developing flower buds.

common_name: Diamond Spire Gardenia (Narrow Columnar Fragrant Gardenia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Diamond Spire is a narrow, upright columnar gardenia cultivar bred for tight spaces where a standard rounded gardenia would be too wide, while still producing the classic fragrant double white flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade, with afternoon shade appreciated in the hottest Gulf Coast gardens. Diamond Spire is a narrow, upright gardenia selection bred to give the intensely fragrant, double white summer flowers of a classic gardenia in a tight, columnar footprint suited to narrow side yards, foundation plantings, and vertical accents where a standard wide-spreading gardenia wouldn't fit. Glossy dark evergreen foliage clothes the upright stems from top to bottom, and the strongly perfumed blooms open over the summer, filling the surrounding air with the classic gardenia scent. Feed with an acid-forming fertilizer in spring and again in early summer, keep soil consistently moist but well drained, and watch for whitefly and sooty mold, common gardenia pests in humid climates. Prune only lightly right after flowering to maintain the narrow form.
